\documentclass[11pt]{article}
\usepackage[margin=1in]{geometry}

\title{Review Essay: The Gilded Cage}
\author{H.~Okafor}
\date{}

\begin{document}
\maketitle

\section{The Book}
\textit{The Gilded Cage} is the third volume of Professor
Almeida's study of court record-keeping under the late
Stuarts, and it is in many ways the most ambitious. Where the
earlier volumes contented themselves with describing the
archive, this one advances a claim about its fabrication:
the records, Almeida argues, were curated to flatter the
restored monarchy, and the gaps in the series are evidence
of suppression rather than of neglect.

\section{The Argument}
The claim rests on a comparison of the surviving docket books
with the registers of the Exchequer, and the comparison is
conducted with considerable ingenuity. Chapter four, which
reconstructs the lost sessions of 1667 from fee receipts
alone, will be required reading for students of the period.
Yet the argument from silence is pressed harder than the
evidence allows. The reviewers found the committee's evidence
\textbf{\emph{strictly \textit{inconclusive}}} and said so
in three separate footnotes, a warning that Almeida cites
without ever quite answering.

\section{The Method}
On matters of method the volume is less assured than its
predecessors. The statistical appendix treats each register
as an independent witness, although the registers share
scribes, share paper stock, and in two cases share a binding.
A reader who turns to \textit{The Gilded Cage} after the
author's exemplary second volume will notice the difference:
where the earlier book tripled its caveats, this one buries
them. The chapter on palaeography is the honourable
exception, and its cautious tone shows what the rest of the
argument might have been.
It is a pity, because the underlying labour is formidable.
The transcriptions alone represent years of work, and the
appendix of variant readings will be quarried by editors
for a generation. Few living scholars could have assembled
this evidence; fewer still would have read it so closely.

\section{Verdict}
None of this diminishes the book's real achievement. No one
has read the docket books more carefully, and no future
historian of the Restoration court will be able to ignore
the map of the archive that these pages provide. But the
map is not the territory, and the silence of the records
is not yet a confession. \textit{The Gilded Cage} deserves
its readers; it also deserved a sterner editor than it had.
A second edition is already promised, and the author has
hinted that the apparatus will be revised in light of the
reviews. That revision will be worth waiting for: the
evidence deserves an argument as careful as the archive
that produced it.
\end{document}
